props.title: Stryker
props.initialSlug: Post-apocalyptic biker gangs battle for water

sections.content: **Stryker** (1983) belongs to the wave of post-apocalyptic exploitation films that flooded theaters after the success of Mad Max (1979). Director Cirio H. Santiago, the Filipino B-movie maestro, crafted this desert wasteland thriller during the height of the post-nuke craze that included The New Barbarians (1983) and **2019: After the Fall of New York** (1983). Like many films of this genre, Stryker centers on battles for water in a scorched future, predating similar themes in **Tank Girl** (1995) and **Waterworld** (1995).

sections.content: Santiago's direction follows the exploitation playbook with car chases, explosions, and makeshift weapons. The film's low budget actually works in its favor, as the Philippine locations provide an authentically desolate backdrop that bigger-budget films like **Spacehunter: Adventures in the Forbidden Zone** (1983) tried to recreate with expensive sets. Steve Sandor's portrayal of Stryker feels deliberately modeled after Mel Gibson's Max Rockatansky, though with a more straightforward revenge motivation.

The film's legacy lives on in its influence on later post-apocalyptic B-movies, particularly in how it established many tropes of the "water as currency" subplot that would become standard in the genre. Its mix of motorcycle gangs, desert fortresses, and scavenged technology would be echoed in countless films like Steel Dawn (1987) and Cherry 2000 (1987). SUBHEAD: Filipino Post-Apocalyptic Cinema

sections.content: **Stryker** represents a significant entry in Filipino exploitation cinema of the 1980s. Santiago, along with producers like Roger Corman, turned the Philippines into a factory for post-apocalyptic action films, including **Wheels of Fire** (1985) and **Raiders of the Sun** (1992). These films utilized the country's varied landscapes and lower production costs to create convincing wasteland settings that rivaled their Hollywood counterparts.
